overview.body:
**Forseti** ​(*forseti*) — ‌Justice, Mediation ‌· ​President, chairman ​— belongs ​to the ​Norse ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Justice, ​Mediation". ‌The name ​means "President, ‌chairman"[^1].

​Forseti is ​the son ​of Baldr ​and ​Nanna, and ‌the quietest ​great ‌office in ​the northern ‌pantheon: ​he owns ‌Glitnir, the ​hall ‌of gold ​pillars and ​silver roof, ‌and ‌every quarrel ‌that comes ​before ​him ends ‌in peace ​— ​Snorri says ‌all who ​bring ​their lawsuits ‌to him ​go away ‌reconciled, ​and Grímnismál ​says he ​dwells ​there day ‌after day ‌and ​puts all ‌suits to ​sleep.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Forseti** ‌and ‌serves its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/forseti/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *forseti* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Younger ​Futhark ​as ​**ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ**. Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"President, ​chairman"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*forseti* ​survives only ‌because ​the ​early ​domain-name ​system could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ​Unicode ‌restoration **Forseti** ‌recovers ‌the ​full ​diacritic detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​directly in ​the ‌address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— ​a ‌description computed ‌from ​the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation ‌runs:

- **f** ‌→ ​**F** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **o** ​→ ‌**o** ​— ​Same
- **r** ​→ ‌**r** ​— ​Same
- ​**s** → ‌**s** ​— ‌Same
- ​**e** → ‌**e** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**t** → ​**t** ​— ​Same
- ​**i** ‌→ **i** ‌— ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the name ‌is **/ˈfor.se.ti/** — ‌Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- **For-** ​— Voiceless labiodental ​[f], short open-mid back ​[ɔ], trilled [r] ​— the preposition for, ‌'before', held brief ​and stressed, as in ​every Old Norse ‌word.
- **-se-** — ​Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] ‌and short front ​[ɛ]; all three vowels ‌of the name ​are short — Old ​Norse marks no ​length here.
- **-ti** ​— Voiceless dental stop ​[t] and short ‌close front [i]; the ​final -i is ‌the weak masculine ending, ​so the name ‌takes no nominative ​-r.

For the modern ‌speaker, the closest ​approximation is: FOR-seh-ti — ‌three short, even ​syllables, stress on the ​first, the r ‌lightly trilled; close ‌to the modern Icelandic ‌pronunciation of forseti, ​'president'.

Kindred and historical ​forms of the ‌name:

- **Old Norse** — ​Forseti — the ​theonym and the ‌common noun forseti, 'chairman, ​president', a transparent ​compound of for, 'before', ‌and seti, 'sitter' ​(cf. sitja, 'to sit')
- ‌**Old Frisian** — ​Fosite, the god of ​the island Fosetesland ​(Heligoland) in Alcuin's ​Life of Willibrord, c. ‌796 — the ‌form Grimm and much ​modern scholarship connect ‌with Forseti
- **Younger Futhark** ​— ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ (f-u-r-s-i-t-i), ​the reconstructed Viking-Age ‌carving; ᚢ writes the ‌o, ᛁ writes ‌both e and i
- ‌**Modern Icelandic** — ​Forseti — the god's ‌name, and since ​1944 the title ​of the head of ​state: Forseti Íslands, ‌the President of Iceland

​Forseti is a ​plain restoration by the ​mechanical rule: the ‌normalized Old Norse ​form is already plain ​ASCII — no ​diacritic, no thorn or ‌eth, nothing for ​the ASCII alphabet to ‌lose. The name ​is a law-term ‌before it is a ​personal name: Old ‌Norse forseti means 'chairman, ‌president', the one ​who sits before the ​assembly, and the ​god is the ​office made personal. Only ‌the capital distinguishes ‌the restored form from ​the input.

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as **ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ**.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration is ​*fursiti*.

The ​rendering proceeds ‌step by ​step:

- ᚠ ​(fé) writes ‌both /f/ ​and /v/
- ‌ᚢ (úr) ​writes the ‌rounded back ​vowels /u, ​o, ​ø, ǫ, ​y/ and ​/w/
- ᚱ ‌(reið) writes ​/r/
- The ‌spelling fursiti ​is a ‌normalized phonetic ​reconstruction; Younger ‌Futhark does ​not distinguish ‌voiced/voiceless stops ​or separate ​short and ‌long vowels

‌The normalized ‌Old ​Norse form ​is **Forseti** ‌— already ​plain ASCII, ​with no ‌diacritic or ​distinctive letter ​for the ‌restoration to ​recover; in ‌the Younger ​Futhark the ​name would ​have been ​carved ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ ‌(f-u-r-s-i-t-i: ᚢ ‌writes the ​o, ‌ᛁ writes ​both e ​and i, ‌and the ‌final -i ‌is the ‌weak masculine ​ending, so ‌the name ​takes no ​nominative ᛦ). ​Because the ‌name is ​pure ASCII, ​its domain ​was registered ‌decades ​ago in ​the ordinary ​way: **forseti.com ‌is held ​by a ‌third party ​outside the ‌PuniCodex collection ​and is ‌watched for ‌release** — ​no form ​of the ​name is ​currently owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

domains.body:
Forseti ​is the ‌son of ‌Baldr and ​Nanna, and ​the quietest ​great office ​in the ​northern pantheon: ‌he owns ​Glitnir, ​the hall ‌of gold ​pillars and ‌silver roof, ​and every ‌quarrel that ​comes before ​him ends ​in peace ​— ​Snorri says ‌all who ​bring their ‌lawsuits to ​him go ‌away reconciled, ​and Grímnismál ‌says he ​dwells ‌there day ​after day ​and puts ‌all suits ‌to sleep.[^1]

### ‌Glitnir

'The ​shining one': ​Forseti's hall, ‌propped with ​gold ​and roofed ‌with silver ​— the ​tenth dwelling ‌in Grímnismál's ​tally of ‌the homes ​of the ​gods.

### The ​Dómstaðr

​The best ‌court of ‌judgment among ​gods and ‌men — ​Snorri's verdict ​on the ‌seat from ‌which every ‌party ‌departs reconciled.

### ​The Spring ‌of Fosetesland

​The holy ​well on ​Heligoland whose ‌water was ​drawn only ​in ​silence — ‌the Frisian ​cult of ​Fosite that ​Alcuin records ‌around 796.

### The ​Title

Forseti, ‌'he who ​sits before': ‌the ​god's name ‌is an ‌office, and ​the office ​outlived the ​god — ​it is ‌Iceland's word ‌for its ​president.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 17 (Glitnir among the heavenly halls) and 32 (Forseti, son of Baldr and Nanna; the best court of judgment among gods and men); Skáldskaparmál þulur (Forseti in the roll of the Æsir).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Forseti ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set of ​recurring ‌attributes, ​each a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**Glitnir** ‌— The ​shining ​hall ​of gold ​pillars ​and ‌silver roof ​— ‌justice ​made architecture
- ‌**The ​dómstaðr** ‌— The ​judgment-seat ‌called ​the best ​among ‌gods ‌and men ‌— ​authority ​measured in ‌reconciled ​parties
- ​**Sátt, the ‌settlement** ​— ​The reconciled ‌departure ​— the ‌Edda's ​one ​statistic about ​Forseti: ​all ‌who come ‌with ​suits ‌go away ​at ​peace
- ‌**The silent ‌spring** ‌— ‌The holy ​water ‌of ​Fosetesland, drawn ​only ​in ‌silence — ​the ​Frisian ​face of ‌the ​settler ​of strife
- ​**The ‌title ​forseti** — ‌'He ​who ‌sits before' ​— ‌the ‌office that ​became ​a ​god, and ​the ‌word ‌that outlived ​him

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

mythology.body:
Forseti has the thinnest ​dossier of any god in the Edda with ‌a hall to his name: one stanza in ‌the Poetic Edda, two sentences in the ​Prose, and not a single adventure. What those ​lines build is nonetheless complete — a god ​whose whole mythology is the thing he does ​to quarrels.[^1]

### The Tenth Hall (Grímnismál 15)

​Grímnismál counts the dwellings of the gods, and ‌the tenth is his: 'Glitnir is the tenth; ​it is propped with gold and thatched ​with silver too, and there Forseti dwells most ‌days and puts all suits to sleep.' The ​verb is the miracle — svæfir, he lulls: ‌not wins, not crushes, but puts to ​sleep, the way one settles a restless child. ‌The poem gives him no weapon, no journey, ​no adversary — only a shining hall ​and the daily practice of ending strife.[^2]

### The ​Best Court Among Gods and Men (Gylfaginning 17 ​· 32)

Snorri builds the same hall ​twice. In the survey of the heavenly places, ‌Glitnir stands with walls, pillars, and posts of ​red gold and a roof of silver. In ‌the catalogue of the Æsir he names ​its owner: the son of Baldr and Nanna, ‌daughter of Nep, is called Forseti; he owns ​that hall in heaven which is called ‌Glitnir, and all who come to him with ​lawsuits go away reconciled — 'that is the ‌best court of judgment among gods and ​men, as it is said here' — and ​Snorri quotes the Grímnismál stanza as his proof. ‌The Prose Edda's whole account of the god ‌is one sentence, and the sentence is ‌enough: the child of the slain best of ​gods sits in the shining hall, and no ​quarrel survives him.

### The Spring on Fosetesland ‌(Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi 10)

The god's name is ​older on parchment than the Eddas by four ​centuries. Around 796, Alcuin tells in his Life ‌of Willibrord how the missionary was driven ​ashore on a Frisian island 'called Fosetesland after ​the god Fosite, whom those peoples worship' — ‌Heligoland, the holy land. The island held ​a sacred spring whose water might be drawn ‌only in silence, and the cattle that grazed ​there were untouchable. Willibrord baptized three men ​in the spring and had some of the ​cattle slaughtered for food; the islanders watched for ​the trespassers to be struck mad or dead, ‌and when nothing happened they dragged the ‌company before King Radbod, who cast lots daily ​for three days. The lot never fell on ‌Willibrord; one of his companions was chosen ​and died for the sacrilege. Whether Frisian Fosite ​and Norse Forseti are one god remains the ‌standing scholarly question — but the island, the ‌silence, and the sanctity are recorded history ‌of the cult.

### The Thirteenth Law-Speaker (Frisian legal ‌tradition)

Late medieval Frisian legal texts preserve a ​foundation legend that Jacob Grimm could not ‌keep away from Fosite. The Frisians, wanting law ​of their own, were set adrift in a ​boat; they prayed, and a thirteenth man ​appeared among the twelve law-speakers, steered them to ‌land, threw a golden axe ashore — and ​where it struck, a spring burst forth — ​and there taught them the law. The ​golden axe, the spring, and the divine lawgiver ‌made the identification irresistible to nineteenth-century scholarship; modern ​readers generally take the thirteenth for Christ, ​the usual stranger of medieval legend. The story ​is kept here for what it genuinely is: ‌proof that the Frisian-speaking world remembered law ​as a gift that came over the water ‌to found a thing-site by a spring.

### The ​Name in the Roll (Þulur · the catalogue ‌tradition)

Where narrative fails, the catalogues keep ​him. The þulur — the mnemonic name-lists of ‌the skaldic tradition — count Forseti in the ‌roll of the Æsir, and Snorri's two ​Glitnir notices carry the hall independently of its ​owner. No saga stages him, no skald builds ​a kenning on him, and yet the name ​never drops out of the lists. The ‌tradition treats him the way law treats a ‌good judge: no stories, only the record that ​the court was held.

syncretism.body:
The standing ​cross-border question ‌is the ‌equation Forseti ​= Fosite. ​Jacob Grimm ​made it, ​and the philology ​keeps it ‌alive: Old ​Norse forseti ​is a ‌transparent folk-formation ​— 'the ‌one who sits ​before' — ‌while Frisian ​Fosite cannot ​be derived ​from it, ​which is why ​Lindow entertains ‌that the ​Norse god ‌was borrowed ​from the ‌Frisian cult, ​the form attested ‌four centuries ​earlier, and ‌re-etymologized into ​a law-term ​on the ‌way north. ‌The Norwegian place-name ‌Forsetlund, 'Forseti's ​grove', shows ​the name ‌lived in ​Scandinavian cult-geography ​whatever its ‌direction of travel. ​Within the ​corpus his ‌true kin ​is Týr, ‌the pantheon's ​other god of ​law: where ​Týr guarantees ​the oath ‌with his ‌right hand ​in the ‌wolf's jaws, Forseti ​dissolves the ​quarrel the ‌oath was ‌sworn to ‌settle. And ‌his own ​house is a ‌study in ​inheritance: Snorri ​says of ​Baldr that ‌none of ​his judgments ​can stand, and ​of Baldr's ‌son that ​no judgment ​of his ​is ever ‌refused — the ​father's flaw ‌retired in ​the son's ‌office.[^1]

Kindred ​figures in ‌the PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index include ​[[maat|Mꜣꜥt]], [[ochosi|Ọṣọọsì]], ​[[shamash|Šamaš]], [[shango|Ṣàngó]], ​and [[var|Vár]], ​each linked ‌through justice ‌/ law ​/ truth.

cultural-legacy.body: Forseti's ​afterlife is ‌the word ‌itself. ​Old Norse ​forseti was ​the ​law-term for ​the presiding ‌judge ​— the ​one who ‌sits ​before the ‌court — ​and ‌when Iceland ​became a ​republic ​in 1944 ​it reached ​for ‌the same ​word ‌for its ​head of ‌state: ​the President ‌of Iceland ​is ‌to this ​day Forseti ​Íslands, ‌and no ‌other god ‌of ​the North ​still signs ‌laws. ​In scholarship, ​the god's ‌single ​sentence in ​Gylfaginning became ‌one ​of the ‌most-quoted passages ​on ​the Norse ​legal imagination, ​the ‌standing citation ‌for the ​proposition ‌that the ​North idealized ​reconciliation ‌over verdict. ‌Modern Heathenry ‌keeps ‌him as ​the patron ‌of ​mediation and ​of disputes ​ended ‌without feud; ​and ​on the ​Frisian side, ‌Heligoland ​— the ​holy land ​— ‌still carries ​the memory ‌of ​the cult ‌in its ​name. ‌He left ‌no image, ​no ​saga, no ​drama: he ​left ‌his title ‌to a ​republic.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

archaeology.body: Forseti ​is a ‌textual and ‌onomastic ​god: no ​runestone ​invokes him, ​no image ​or ‌amulet names ​him, ​and no ‌votive deposit ​can ‌be laid ​at ‌his hall. ​The ground ​evidence ​is the ​place-name: ​Forsetlund, 'Forseti's ‌grove', in ​Vestfold ‌near the ​Oslo ‌fjord, attests ​that the ‌name ​lived in ‌Scandinavian ​cult-geography and ​not only ‌in ‌Icelandic books. ‌The ​Frisian witness ​is earlier ‌than ​any Norse ​manuscript: ‌Alcuin's Life ​of Willibrord ​(c. ‌796) preserves ​the ‌island Fosetesland ​— Heligoland, ​'holy ​land' — ​with ‌its silent ‌spring and ​sacred ‌herd, the ​only ​near-contemporary description ‌of the ‌cult ‌site of ‌the ​god-name's continental ‌form. The ​Norse ​literary witnesses ​are ‌the Codex ​Regius (Grímnismál) ​and ​the fourteenth-century ‌codices ​of the ​Prose Edda. ​The ‌Younger Futhark ​rendering ‌ᚠᚢᚱᛋᛁᛏᛁ is ​a normalized ‌reconstruction ​of how ‌the ‌name would ​have been ​carved; ​no Viking-Age ​inscription ‌of the ‌theonym is ​known.[^1]

meditation.body: Forseti ​is the ‌patron of ‌the outcome ​the sagas ​almost ​never reach: ​the quarrel ​that ends. ‌The heroic ​literature ​of the ‌North is ​a literature ‌of feud ​— ‌insult answered ​by wound, ​wound by ​killing, killing ​by ​lawsuit, lawsuit ‌by ambush ​— and ‌into ​that world ‌the Edda ​sets one ‌shining hall ​where ‌the arithmetic ​stops. All ​who come ‌with their ‌cases ‌go away ​reconciled: it ​is the ‌only perfect ​record ​in the ‌corpus, and ​it belongs ​to the ‌son ​of the ‌god whose ​own judgments ​could not ​stand. ​The tradition ‌seems to ‌know what ​it was ‌asking. ​Reconciliation is ​not the ‌absence of ‌justice but ‌its ‌completion — ​the verdict ‌both parties ​can live ​inside ​— and ‌the god ​who delivers ​it ​is given ‌nothing else: ​no weapon, ​no journey, ​no ‌death, no ​prophecy. His ‌silence is ​the teaching. ‌In ​a mythology ‌that counts ‌its heroes ​by what ​they ​break, Forseti ​counts by ‌what he ‌puts to ​sleep.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Forseti in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Forseti within the cosmological drama of justice.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Forseti attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

prose-edda.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Forseti for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Forseti as justice. The restoration Forseti keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

runic-evidence.body:
Direct runic attestations of Forseti are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').

sagas.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Forseti alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as justice in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Forseti marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 15 (Glitnir, 'propped with gold and thatched with silver'; Forseti, who 'puts all suits to sleep').
